implementation_notes: C has no coroutine support, and the two realisations are both manual. ucontext (makecontext/swapcontext) gives a stackful coroutine: each coroutine gets its own allocated stack, swapcontext saves and restores the machine context, and any function can yield at any depth. The cost is stack memory per coroutine and non-portability (makecontext is POSIX, deprecated on some platforms, and not available on Windows). The stackless form is a hand-written state machine - a switch on an enum storing the resume point and the locals in a struct - which is portable but verbose and forces the call chain to be rewritten. A third form is a separate thread per coroutine with condition variables, which is simple but defeats the purpose (the memory cost of a thread). For most C programs the honest answer is threads or an event loop with callbacks, because a hand-rolled coroutine is a large amount of unsafe code for a saving.
idiom_name: ucontext (makecontext/swapcontext) for a stackful coroutine, or a hand-written state machine for a stackless one
pitfalls: makecontext is POSIX and deprecated on some platforms, and is unavailable on Windows - the stackful form is not portable.
Each stackful coroutine costs its stack (often 64 KB here), so thousands of them is tens of megabytes - the reason Go grows stacks on demand instead.
A coroutine must be resumed from the same thread if it touches thread-local state or a lock held across the swap; migrating it is undefined behaviour in this hand-rolled form.
Forgetting to free the stack leaks it per coroutine, and a coroutine that is never resumed holds its stack forever.
alternative: A thread per coroutine with condition variables (simple but costly), or a callback-based event loop (no coroutines but deeply nested)
